claim: Three nested common-in-neighbourhood deletions leave the coefficient of log2 log2 N equal to 1. For stage lengths s1, s2, s3 and out-degree excesses δi, the count produces γ ≤ log2 N + Π − log2(log2 N − s_eff) + C + o(1), where Π ≥ 0 and 0 ≤ s_eff ≤ s1 + s2 + s3. That expression is at least the one-level bound log2 N − log2 log2 N + C + o(1). It never has the shape log2 N − 2 log2 log2 N + O(1), because that would require log2 N − s_eff at least a constant times (log2 N)^2, while log2 N − s_eff is at most log2 N. Inverted, the lower estimate of f(n) stays of the shape (c + o(1)) n 2^n. Erdős problem 902 is not solved.
definitions: A tournament has one directed edge between every two distinct vertices. For a set S, D(S) is the set of vertices outside S that beat every member of S. A set H dominates a tournament when every vertex outside H is beaten by some vertex of H. γ is the size of a smallest dominating set, and γ of the empty tournament is 0. f(n) is the least order of a tournament in which every n-set has nonempty dominator set; equivalently, f(n) is the least order of a tournament with γ > n. N denotes the order of the tournament whose domination number is being bounded. log2 is the base-2 logarithm. B is any function satisfying B(m) ≤ log2 m − log2 log2 m + C for an absolute constant C and all sufficiently large m, and B(m) ≤ m for smaller m. Section 1 of proof/FN_GAP_ATTEMPT.md supplies one such B, with the constant −log2(c*) absorbed into C. A stage length si is a nonnegative integer. At a tournament of order m, δ ≥ 0 means that every out-degree is at most (1/2 + δ)m. The effective deletion and the penalty of a stage are s_eff,i = si (1 − log2(1 + 2δi)) and πi = si log2(1 + 2δi). Then Π = π1 + π2 + π3 and s_eff = s_eff,1 + s_eff,2 + s_eff,3. The coefficient of the second logarithm is the number c in an upper bound of the shape log2 N − c log2 log2 N + O(1).
argument:
The one-level shape of B is an input. The result is the three-stage composition.

One deletion. Let U be a tournament on m vertices whose out-degrees are at most (1/2 + δ)m, and let 1 ≤ s < m/2. For a uniform s-set S and a vertex v outside S, the probability that S lies in the out-neighbourhood of v is at most the product from i = 0 to s − 1 of ((1/2 + δ)m − i)/(m − 1 − i). Each factor is at most (1/2 + δ)(1 + O(s/m)), so the product is at most (1/2 + δ)^s exp(O(s^2/m)). Averaging over S gives a set with |D(S)| ≤ m (1/2 + δ)^s exp(O(s^2/m)). Every vertex outside S ∪ D(S) is beaten by S, and no vertex of D(S) is beaten by S. If H dominates the induced tournament on D(S), then S ∪ H dominates U. Thus γ(U) ≤ s + γ(U[D(S)]). In particular γ(U) ≤ s + B(|D(S)|) once the remainder is large enough for the logarithmic form of B, and γ(U) ≤ s + |D(S)| otherwise.

The same inequality with the outer s removed is false. In the cyclic triangle, γ = 2. For S a single vertex, D(S) is the unique vertex that beats S, and S ∪ D(S) induces a 2-vertex tournament of domination number 1. The outside vertex is beaten by S, not by that one-vertex dominating set. The bound that matches the deletion is 1 + 1 = 2.

Three deletions. Apply the one-deletion step inside the successive remainders. As long as each remainder is large and the stage length is o of its square root, γ(T) ≤ s1 + s2 + s3 + B(m3), where m3 is the order of the third remainder. Write ρi = 1 − log2(1 + 2δi). Then 0 ≤ ρi ≤ 1 for δi in [0, 1/2], (1/2 + δi)^{si} = 2^{−ρi si}, and si = ρi si + πi. The three size bounds multiply to m3 ≤ N · 2^{−s_eff} · exp(η), where η is the sum of the three O(si^2/m) terms and tends to 0 in the stated range. The map m ↦ log2 m − log2 log2 m is increasing for m > 4, so the largest remainder gives the weakest upper bound. Substituting it yields γ(T) ≤ log2 N + Π − log2(log2 N − s_eff) + C + o(1), provided s_eff ≤ log2 N − ω(1) so that the remainder tends to infinity. If a stage length is large enough that si^2 is not o of the current order, cap the remainder by the order itself. The cap deletes nothing and returns the input bound B.

The third level has no new parameter. The right-hand side depends on the three lengths only through Π and s_eff. Equal lengths (10, 10, 10) and a single length (0, 0, 30) produce the same expression when every δi vanishes. A third stage is a redistribution of one total deletion.

Comparison. For Π ≥ 0 and 0 ≤ s_eff < log2 N, log2(log2 N − s_eff) ≤ log2 log2 N, so log2 N + Π − log2(log2 N − s_eff) ≥ log2 N − log2 log2 N. The gap is exactly Π + log2(log2 N / (log2 N − s_eff)) and is nonnegative. Thus no choice of lengths or excesses beats the one-level expression.

Coefficient. If s_eff = o(log2 N) and Π = o(1), the gap tends to 0, and the bound is log2 N − log2 log2 N + C + o(1). The coefficient is 1, and the constant is the constant already present in B. If s_eff = α log2 N for a fixed α in (0, 1), the second logarithm is log2 log2 N + log2(1 − α). The coefficient is still 1, and the upper bound exceeds the one-level bound by Π − log2(1 − α) = Π + log2(1/(1 − α)) > 0. If s_eff = log2 N − β log2 log2 N for fixed β > 0, the bound becomes log2 N − log2 log2 log2 N − log2 β + Π + o(1), which is weaker than coefficient 1 by about log2 log2 N. If s_eff ≥ log2 N − O(1), the remainder is bounded and γ ≤ s1 + s2 + s3 + O(1). Since each ρi ≤ 1, the sum of the lengths is at least s_eff, and the bound is at least log2 N + O(1), again weaker than coefficient 1 by a full log2 log2 N.

Coefficient 2 is impossible inside this shape. Suppose log2 N + Π − log2(log2 N − s_eff) ≤ log2 N − 2 log2 log2 N + K for a fixed K and arbitrarily large N, with s_eff < log2 N. Rearrangement gives log2(log2 N − s_eff) ≥ 2 log2 log2 N − K + Π. Since Π ≥ 0, the logarithmic remainder log2 N − s_eff is at least 2^{−K} (log2 N)^2. It is also at most log2 N. For every N with log2 N > 2^K those two bounds disagree. If instead s_eff ≥ log2 N, the remainder is bounded and the estimate falls back to a bound of size at least log2 N + O(1), which is weaker than coefficient 1.

A large excess does not open another route to coefficient 2 in the uniform bound. If some out-degree is (1/2 + δ)m for a fixed δ in (0, 1/2), one vertex leaves an in-neighbourhood of size at most (1/2 − δ)m + O(1), and γ ≤ 1 + B of that order. Three such greedy steps give log2 N − log2 log2 N + O_δ(1). The coefficient remains 1. A vertex of in-degree at most N/log2 N does give a coefficient-2 estimate on that one tournament: the in-neighbourhood has log-order log2 N − log2 log2 N, and B then contributes a second copy of log2 log2 N, while the added vertex is only 1. A regular tournament has no such vertex. The bound asserted for every tournament has to cover the regular case, and on that case the three-level count stays at coefficient 1. The quantity f(n) is determined by the maximum of γ, so an improvement on irregular tournaments does not raise the lower estimate of f(n).

Inversion. Suppose every tournament of order N satisfies γ ≤ log2 N − log2 log2 N + C + o(1). Then γ ≤ n whenever log2 N − log2 log2 N + C ≤ n. The largest such N has log2 N = n + log2 n + O(1), hence N = (2^{−C} + o(1)) n 2^n. The three-level count therefore gives f(n) ≥ (2^{−C} + o(1)) n 2^n and does not give f(n) ≥ (c + o(1)) n^2 2^n. The passage from one factor of n to two factors of n is exactly the passage from coefficient 1 to coefficient 2. That passage does not occur.

Erdős problem 902 is not solved. The count does not determine f(4), and it does not narrow the gap between n 2^n and n^2 2^n.

evidence.inequality_kept: γ ≤ |S| + γ(T[D(S)]). The cyclic triangle has γ = 2; deleting the outer vertex from the bound drops it to 1, which is false.
evidence.closed_form: With every δi = 0, the three-level expression is log2 N − log2(log2 N − (s1 + s2 + s3)).
evidence.split_does_not_matter: (10,10,10) and (0,0,30) return the same value, so the third stage is not an independent saving.
evidence.hand_check: log2(1021) = 10 + log2(1 − 3/1024). With log2(1 − x) ≈ −x/ln 2 and x = 3/1024, the correction is about 0.00423, and 1024 − (10 − 0.00423) = 1014.00423, matching the (1,1,1) row.
evidence.what_was_not_run: No tournament search and no recomputation of c*. The numerical rows only evaluate the closed form.

weaknesses: The status proved applies only to this negative statement: three nested deletions do not change the coefficient. The shape of B is taken from the one-level bound and is not re-proved. The o(1) needs the order tending to infinity and each stage length o of the square root of the current order; outside that range the remainder is capped and the count falls back to B. The argument says nothing about a one-step count of every n-set. A tournament with a very small in-neighbourhood can satisfy a stronger numerical bound, and that bound is not available for a regular tournament, so it does not improve f(n). The constant in front of n 2^n is whatever constant B already carries. Erdős problem 902 stays open, and f(4) is not evaluated.

next_step: Stop. The third deletion level leaves the coefficient of log2 log2 N equal to 1, for every split of the stage lengths and every out-degree excess. A further deletion of the same kind has the same shape.
relation_to_prior: One-level counting past c* and two-stage averaging are exhausted. This is the third deletion level: three successive common-in-neighbourhoods, then the input bound B. It does not re-derive c*, and it does not stop at one auxiliary set. The exhausted keys claim-L-single-pair-link, one-level-counting-past-cstar, two-stage-averaging-second-log, random-cayley-beat-erdos-upper, n51-local-milp-certificates, and wrong-direction-covering-local48 are not repeated. The new comparison is the nonnegative gap Π + log2(log2 N / (log2 N − s_eff)), which covers every triple of lengths at once.
novelty: The three-stage expansion shows that s1, s2, and s3 enter only as an effective deletion and a nonnegative penalty. Every such choice sits at least as high as the one-level bound, and coefficient 2 would require the deleted remainder to exceed (log2 N)^2 while the order supplies only log2 N. The split of the lengths is invisible in the final expression. This is a constraint on iterated deletion. It is not a new estimate of f(n).
